metadata.notes: SolarWinds SUNBURST supply chain compromise (December 2020). Attack path: #10 ||[update][@Vendor→@Org]|| →[Δt=instant] #7 + [DRE: C] →[Δt=~14d] #4 →[Δt=~2h] #1 + [DRE: C]. APT29/Cozy Bear attributed (Axiom IV: actor identity does not change cluster classification). Sources: CISA Alert AA20-352A, Microsoft MSRC, FireEye/Mandiant UNC2452 report.

path_sequence.notes: Trust Acceptance Event: SolarWinds Orion update v2019.4-2020.2.1 containing SUNBURST backdoor accepted and installed by target organization via legitimate update channel. The compromised DLL (SolarWinds.Orion.Core.BusinessLayer.dll) was digitally signed by SolarWinds, passing all trust verification. Falsifiability test: removing the third-party trust link (not accepting the update) would have prevented this step.

FEC execution via designed capability: SUNBURST backdoor DLL loaded and executed by the legitimate SolarWinds Orion service (solarwinds.businesslayerhost.exe). The execution used the environment's intended DLL loading mechanism — an intended data→code transition, not an exploit. SUNBURST remained dormant for approximately 12-14 days before activating C2 communication via DNS (avsvmcloud.com). R-EXEC satisfied: FEC execution recorded as #7. [DRE: C] is recorded here: host and domain profiling was sent to the C2 channel, and the SAML token-signing certificate was obtained during this step. Per Axiom X the acquisition of credential material maps to the enabling cluster, which is this #7 step, so the confidentiality event belongs here and not on the #4 step that later presents the forged token.

Credential application: attacker forged SAML tokens using stolen signing certificates to impersonate legitimate users and access cloud resources (Azure AD, Office 365). Per Axiom X and R-CRED, the acquisition of the signing key occurred during the #7 step and its confidentiality event is recorded there; the USE of forged credentials to authenticate is always #4 regardless of acquisition method. This step carries no DRE of its own: authenticating discloses nothing, alters nothing and denies nothing. The disclosure it enables is recorded where it occurs, on the #1 step that reads mail through the designed cloud APIs — attaching [DRE: C] here as well would count the same exfiltration twice and would judge the step by what the attacker later obtained rather than by what this step did.

Abuse of legitimate cloud functions: attacker used valid (forged) credentials to abuse Azure AD APIs, Office 365 mail reading APIs, and federated trust configurations for data exfiltration. No code flaw exploited — the attacker operated within the designed functionality of the cloud platform using stolen identity. Data stayed data; no foreign code was introduced at this stage.
